en: In the Śrī Bhāgavata-sandarbha, the first is the Tattva-sandarbha; Śrī Kṛṣṇa is victorious!

The wise indeed worship Him who is dark-complexioned yet not black by luster, together with His limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and attendants, primarily through sacrifices consisting of congregational chanting (saṅkīrtana). //1// [BhP 11.5.32] Victory to Śrī Kṛṣṇa!
In Him who is the Lord of Dharma, whose name brings salvation to the universe, who takes delight even in a mere semblance of devotion,
and whose nature is eternal bliss and non-dual consciousness;
May our delight always abide in that reality.
He who, by means of the networks of rays from the words of the Vedas, utterly destroyed that mass of darkness known as Māyāvāda,
and by whom devotion to Viṣṇu was demonstrated to the world.
May this Bhānu Ānandatīrtha be victorious!
Those two supreme knowers of reality, who on this earth demonstrated that the truth is like a jewel held in the hand— namely, Govinda, whose feet are resorted to by Indirā— [have revealed it].
We ever praise those two noble jewels, Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana, who are like two suns to the mass of thick darkness of the doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda), and who have created wonders.
He who, with the nectar of his speech, restored the pure Maheśvara— whose radiance had been obscured by the mud of Sāṅkhya, the dust of fallacious reasoning, and the pit of illusory transformation.
May that Lord Kṛṣṇa be our refuge, O Jīva.
Since men might fail to engage with this extensive treatise due to indolence,
a brief commentary is being published here upon this profound composition.
Those very readings which were refined by the illustrious Jīva in this compendium are here explained; no others are taken up that were neglected by him.
The venerable Śrī Bādarāyaṇa Vyāsa, having illuminated the Brahma-sūtras and manifested the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam as their commentary, instructed Śuka in it;
in order to determine its meaning—

Śrījīva, the god of love, performs an auspicious invocation with the word "Kṛṣṇa"— which is a thunderbolt against the mountain ranges of obstacles and a cloud of desired nectar— pointing toward his own cherished object;
he was thus questioned by King Nimi regarding his hand...

Having addressed the worthy practitioner by saying, "I have described the descents of the Yugas beginning with the Truth-age; now hear how it is even in the Kali age," he made him attentive and said, "The dark-complexioned one.
Wise people worship Hari even in the Kali age.
By what means? He says: "by sacrifices consisting primarily of chanting and by acts of worship.
Of what nature is he? He says: "he whose internal color (varṇa) is black"—the word "whose form" (rūpa) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.

By "splendor" (tviṣā) is meant "not black" due to its radiance; for Garga had said, "White, red, and yellow have now turned black. Thus, by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), the meaning is that he is as fair as lightning.
The limbs are Nityānanda and Advaita; the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) are Śrīvāsa and others;
the weapons are the names of the Lord because they sever ignorance; and the attendants (pārṣadas) are...
"Gadādhara, Govinda,
and others"— by the inclusion of "together with them," his great strength is manifested. Thus it is in the words of Garga.
"He is yellow" is said with reference to His previous incarnations;
this incarnation should be understood as occurring in the Kali age of the twenty-eighth Vaivasvata Manvantara within the Śvetavarāha Kalpa.
Because the dharma was seen as it was taught by Śrī Caitanya himself there,
whereas among others in the Kali age, it appears in some places as dark and in others as yellowish-red.
Because manifestation is described as having the appearance of a leaf;
and because it is said, "In the Kali age you became concealed" (BhP 7.9.38), and "White,
red, and likewise yellow" (BhP 10.8.13).
And it is said: "Listen likewise even in the Kali age" (BhP 11.5.31).
Those who reflect upon this are the truly wise.
Furthermore, "being concealed" should be understood as being veiled by the splendor of the Beloved.
The figures here that differ from those of the preceding act are indicators of the sequence of the commentary (ṭippanī);
these should be understood as having two dots, whereas the figures indicating the subject matter (viṣaya) are without dots.
In this work, the even-numbered figures indicate the chapters on the aggregates (skandha) as designated by the authors;
those other than these have been devised by us for the purpose of understanding the sequence of the annotations.

Those [numerals] which follow the words denoting the objects (viṣaya) have two dots at their head; however, those which are the digits themselves should be understood as having no dot at their head. //1//

We have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇacaitanya, who is dark within and fair without, who has manifested the glory of his limbs and other attributes, and who is worshipped in the Kali age through congregational chanting and other means. //2//
BD: Under the guise of a commentary on the verses of Kṛṣṇavarṇa, he resorts to that very meaning [of the *Bhagavadgītā*] with the words "inside" (*antar*).
The meaning is clear. //2//
Victory to Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana on the land of Mathurā, who, as the authors of this manuscript, reveal the ultimate reality. (3)
BD: Now, he performs an auspicious rite in the form of a benediction and a salutation with the words "May they be victorious.
May my Guru and Paramaguru—possessing the splendor of knowledge, dispassion, and austerity, and endowed with eternal beauty—be ever victorious.
Of those manifesting their own excellence;
"on the land of Mathurā"— therein lies their direct supervision.

It is manifested; it is thus wished that victory may belong to those two. Here, the verb *ji* (to conquer) expresses the excellence of those two over all other multitudes of virtuous beings, because they are the locus of that excellence.
The state of being worthy of universal homage is implied; and it is also suggested that, because he is included within "all," those two [the body and speech] are bowed down by himself.
He states what those two were like: "Those two who caused me to engage in the writing of this manuscript, which is called a *samdarbha*."
The expression "this" (*imām*) is used because [the truth] is established in the intellect (*buddhi*).
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "truth" (*tattva*) may mean a signifier, a category of debate, one's own nature, or the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that they intend to make the Supreme Lord, along with his retinue, known. The suffix *ṇvul* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) for the future tense;
however, the prohibition of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-niṣedhaḥ*) follows from the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70). //3//
A certain Bhaṭṭa, a kinsman of his born from a lineage of southern brahmins, having investigated it, wrote this book based on what was written by the elder Vaiṣṇavas. //4//
BD: Someone says that the work is ancient and has been refined by himself.
"Tad-bāndhava" means Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, the kinsman of those two who possess eternal forms.
Having discerned that [truth] from the works written by the elder Vaiṣṇavas such as Śrī Madhva and others, and having reflected upon it and extracted the essence,
he composed this book. //4//
Having thoroughly examined Jīvaka’s original manuscript—which was disordered, missing, and fragmentary—and having rearranged it, he writes it down. //5//
BD: Having examined the original ancient manuscript of that Bhaṭṭa, Jīvaka, characterized by his mastery [of the subject], having rearranged it and established the sequence,
writes it down in the composition of the work.
It belongs to the *caurādika* group.
From that [root], by Pāṇini 3.3.107 (*ṇyāsa-śrantha*),
the suffix *yuc* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), resulting in *granthanā*.
A "grantha" is a book; its "lekha" is the act of writing it, the suffix *ghañ* being used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
He asks what kind of "lekha" it is, and answers:
"krānta," meaning arranged in sequence.
"Transgressed" means existing out of order; "fragmented" means cut asunder—thus there is the meaningfulness of one's own exertion. //5//
Only he who possesses the singular longing to worship the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should behold this; an oath is hereby given to others.
BD: He states the secret nature of the work with the words "He who [is Śrī...
etc.; for if another were to disregard the supremacy of Kṛṣṇa, misfortune would befall him.
This is for the sake of that auspiciousness, and not out of fear of the faults of the text; for it has been examined by those well-versed [in logic] as being faultless. //6//
Now, having bowed to the mantra-gurus and the gurus who bestow the meaning of the Bhāgavata, I desire to write this compendium, the Śrī-Bhāgavata-sandarbha. //7//

BD: "Now" (*atha*) signifies the revelation of what was hidden; "essence" (*sāra*) refers to the most excellent statement; likewise, "possessing manifold meanings," "being knowable," and "composition" (*sandarbha*) are described by the wise.
Thus, I desire—that is, I wish—to write this composition whose characteristics have been stated by the learned authorities;
for here the *Śrī-Bhāgavata* is being composed (*sandṛbhyate*), meaning it is being strung together (*grathyate*). [The suffix] *hal*...
And by [the rule] *ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.21), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*). //7//
He whose name is "Brahman" appears in some portion of the Veda, whose mere existence as pure consciousness manifests through his own parts while bringing Māyā under his control,
and whose single form known as Nārāyaṇa shines in the supreme ether; [to Him, I bow].
May that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself bestow love here upon those who have taken refuge at His feet. //8//
BD: Now, in order to generate interest in the listener, he first states the subject matter and other ancillary elements of the work briefly, beginning with the words "yasya" (of whom).
He is the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
In this world, may He bestow—that is, grant—love directed toward Himself upon those who have attained His feet, those who serve His lotus-like feet.
Who is He? To this he says: [He is] Śrī... [of Him] who is distinguished by His essential nature, its inherent attributes, form, qualities, and opulences.

Of Kṛṣṇa: existence as pure consciousness (*cinmātra-sattā*), which is the state of being present in the form of knowledge with its various specific attributes unmanifested; [as it is said] in a certain Vedic scripture: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."
In such scriptural passages as "It is to be perceived as 'it exists'" (TaittU 2.1.1) and "He is" (KaṭhU 2.3.13), it receives the designation "Brahman."

The meaning is that for those who contemplate her in such a manner, she is perceived as such. However, it should be understood that for those whose minds are permeated by devotion (*bhakti*), she alone— her various specific attributes being manifested— is perceived as the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*).
Because that which was introduced as "truth and knowledge" is indeed described as the person consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-puruṣa*),
it is therefore said in your hymn: "Victory to you."
"You have no form, nor appearance, nor weapons, nor abode;
nevertheless, you manifest in the form of a person to your devotees.
This must be stated as having been accepted by the ancients in this manner.
Because, according to the manner already stated, even that [liberation] is not undesired;
for by him, Kṛṣṇa, whose portion is the person (puruṣa), while indeed bringing māyā under his own control—
He manifests through his portions;
he is the thousand-headed Puruṣa who reclines upon the ocean of causes, Saṅkarṣaṇa, the portion of Kṛṣṇa, and the lord of Prakṛti.
While keeping her under his control, he, agitated by the sight of her,
emitted eggs; and into their wombs, which were half-filled with waters, [he entered] as the thousand-headed one.
Pradyumna, by means of his own portions such as the Fish and others,
"vibhavati"— that is to say, he manifests the incarnations known as vibhavas, which are characterized by divine play (līlā).
He is that very Kṛṣṇa, whose one principal form, known as Nārāyaṇa,
shines in the supreme ether situated outside the eight coverings.

The meaning is that Nārāyaṇa is his *vilāsa* (manifestation). Since the Lord himself is independent of anything else and generally possesses qualities and powers equal to him, yet differs from him in form and other attributes, he is called a *vilāsa*; all this is thus explained.
This will become clearly manifest in the fourth section; it should be observed. //8//

Now, for the sake of determining the meanings indicated above— namely, the subject matter consisting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and His relationship characterized as the signifier and the signified, the injunction consisting of worship characterized as His service, and the purpose consisting of love for Him— the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) is first determined. In that regard:

Because the person is corrupted by the fourfold defects such as delusion and so forth, and because he is consequently utterly unfit to contact an object whose nature is supramundane and inconceivable, his perceptions and other means of knowledge are likewise defective. //9//
BD: "Then, thus" means of the four who have been indicated and manifested;
and Śrī Kṛṣṇa also.
The subject matter of the treatise; the relationship characterized by that which is expressed and that which expresses it; and the practice thereof.
That which is to be performed— namely, hearing, chanting, and so forth, characterized by that [devotion]— and that which is to be expressed in its ritual worship,
as well as the goal characterized by love for Him, is the supreme human end (*puruṣārtha*).
Regarding names: synonymy (paryāyatva) is the state of having a single denotatum as their denotative object.
That which has a common synonym is "saparyāya" (having a synonym).

The bahuvrīhi compound *samānārta* is formed from the compound with the word *saha*; it is an *asvapada-vigraha* [compound whose analysis does not employ its own constituent words]. By the rule *vopasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.82), the substitution of *sā-* for *saha-* occurs.
The word *saha* is recorded as being used in the senses of totality, simultaneity, prosperity,
similarity, existence, and relationship.
Thus says Śrīdhara.
In that context, because even a worldly person who is intellectually proficient is seized by defects such as delusion and the like,
and because he is therefore unfit to touch such a single ultimate reality, his perceptions and other means of knowledge [do not reach it].
The phrase "possessing faults" (sadoṣāṇi) should be applied [to the means of knowledge].
Delusion, negligence, the desire to deceive, and incapacity of the instruments— these are the four faults in a living being.

Error (*bhrama*) is the cognition of something as being that which it is not; for example, the cognition of a person in a post. Negligence (*pramāda*), characterized by lack of attention and a distracted mind, is the failure to exercise discernment.
The singing that is being performed nearby is not perceived;
this is a desire for deception, an intent to mislead.
That by which even an object known to oneself is not revealed is sensory dullness, which is the inefficiency of the instruments [of perception].
That by which an object is not correctly discerned even when the mind is directed toward it—
these are the defects of the cognizing subject and the living being.
They move among the atoms; in those [atoms],
there are the three— error and so forth— in perception and in the inference based upon it.
However, it should be understood that "word" (śabda) refers to deceptive intent. There are eight means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), beginning with perception (pratyakṣa).
Among these, [perception] is that which is in contact with the object.
The sense organs, such as the eye, are perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Inference (*anumāna*) is the instrument for inferential cognition (*anumiti*);
the knowledge of fire and so forth is inferential cognition (*anumiti*). (Tarka-saṅgraha)
The instrument for that [perception] is the cognition of smoke and so forth; verbal testimony is the word of a reliable person;
and the instrument for analogical cognition is comparison. (Ibid.)

In cases such as "the gavaya is similar to a cow," the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the object named is comparison (*upamiti*); the instrument for that [knowledge] is... (as cited).

Cognition of similarity [is comparison]. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of another fact that serves as a means of proof, based on the observation of a fact that would otherwise be inexplicable; for example, when one who does not eat during the day is fat, this leads to the presumption of his eating at night, thereby establishing the point to be proven. Non-existence (*abhāva*)—

Apprehension through non-perception (*grāhikānupalabdhi*): for example, as the absence of a jar is apprehended on the ground by the non-perception of a jar. Possibility (*sambhava*) is the notion of possibility in the mind, such as "a hundred may exist within a thousand. [The term] *ajñāta-*...
Aitihya (tradition) is that which is well-known through a succession of speakers, such as "there is a yakṣa in this tree. Thus there are eight [types of verbal testimony]. //9//

Therefore, since those [other means] are not authoritative, for us who desire to know that reality which transcends all, is the refuge of all, and is by nature utterly inconceivable and marvelous, the Veda alone— characterized by speech that is non-material (aprākṛta)— is the source of all worldly and transcendental knowledge, established through the lineage of all persons from time immemorial.
The means of valid cognition. //10//
BD: "Then those [means] are not valid cognitions" means that,
due to their connection with defects such as error and the like,
those [means], such as direct perception and so forth, do not become instruments for valid cognition in the ultimate sense.
In the case of seeing a magically conjured head, the perception that "this is indeed his head" is fallacious;
likewise, [the inference] from rain at that time—
Furthermore, when the fire has been extinguished on a mountain that continues to emit smoke for a long time, the inference "there is fire because there is smoke" is seen to be fallacious;
and the same applies to the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*).
Because a meaning established by one authoritative sage has been refuted by another such [sage],
it is said: "He is not a seer (ṛṣi) whose [word is thus]."
The view is that [the means of knowledge] are not distinct;
thus, because these primary ones are inherently flawed, it is well established that those which depend upon them— such as comparison (upamāna) and the rest— are likewise so.
Furthermore, the word of a reliable person is indeed a means of valid cognition for grasping worldly objects, as in cases such as "there is snow on the Himalayas.
And that [cognition], "You are the tenth," is independent of both of those.

In such cases as these, that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for attaining both [perception and inference] is like the movement of the planets through the zodiacal signs. Furthermore, when supported by the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*), those two together are the means of valid cognition (*pramāpaka*). This has been observed before.

Just as when a man who is a deceptive shaveling is not trusted even regarding the truth, there is direct perception supported by a voice from the sky saying, "This is indeed his shaven head"; [so too is it said:
"O you afflicted by cold, do not go on this path."

For example, one might perceive that the fire has been extinguished by rain, yet receive the support of inference through the words of a reliable person stating, "However, that fire is on this smoke-emitting mountain."

Thus, it has been stated that perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition; as Manu says: "One who desires purity in dharma must thoroughly understand this triad: perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions" (Manu 12.105).
In this way, our elders and all those born from Brahmā— gods, humans, and so forth— in every single lineage throughout the entire succession [of teachers].
According to the Viśvakośa, "paramparā" means sequence, lineage, and sometimes killing;
worldly knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) refers to the science of ritual action (*karma-vidyā*).

Supramundane knowledge is the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), as indicated by the Vedic verse: "O Virūpa, with your eternal, non-material speech" (RV 8.75.6). "Speech, without beginning or end, eternal, was emitted by the Self-existent One."
In the beginning, she was divine and composed of the Vedas, from whom all activities proceed.
And because of this traditional teaching (Mbh 12.231.56–57), the rest is clear. //10//
And that [Brahman] is followed by the statement, "Because reasoning has no foundation" (VS 2.1.11), and so forth;
and by the statement, "Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be joined with reasoning" (MBh 6.5.12), and so forth; and because [the Veda] is the source of the Śāstra (VS 1.1.3).
In such passages as these; and in such passages as "But because the Veda is the source of the word" (VS 2.1.27); and:

"O Lord, the Veda is the eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; it is the means of attaining the highest good regarding matters not perceived by the senses, as well as regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful. (BhP 11.20.4)
BD: If it is asked, "But what is this insistence that for us the Veda alone is the authority? he says in response:
"And that is approved," with the words "by Śrī Vyāsa and others" being understood as the ellipsis.
Regarding that, he says "tarka" and so forth,
ending with "sādhya-sādhanayor api";
"tarka" refers to a section of the Brahma-sūtras.
Its meaning is as follows:
the determination of ultimate reality does not occur through reasoning, because that [reasoning] lacks a firm foundation due to the diversity of human intellects.
Thus says the Śruti: "This wisdom is not to be attained by reasoning; it must be taught by another for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.9).
This is stated by means of a pervasive superimposition.
Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the imposition of the pervader (*vyāpaka-āropa*), taking such a form as: "If this were without fire, then it would be without smoke."
And since that [reasoning], by dispelling doubt regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*),
would become a constituent factor of inference, therefore inference is to be grasped by means of reasoning (*tarka*).
"Inconceivable" (*acintyāḥ*)...
It was seen on the occasion of the Udyoga-parvan.
"Śāstra" refers to the Brahma-sūtra.
"Not so"—this is drawn forth [from the previous context]. It is to be meditated upon.

When there is doubt as to whether Hari is to be known through inference or through the Upaniṣads, the scriptural statement "He is to be reflected upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6) suggests that He is to be known through inference; yet, it is established that Hari is not to be known through inference. Why?
Because His source—the means of knowledge—is the scripture, namely the Upaniṣads. Thus, He is known through that.
For the Śruti begins with the words: "I ask you about the person known from the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
"But on account of scripture" (śrutes tu), this is Brahma-sūtra 2.1.17. The word "no" (na) is understood from the preceding context.
Defects such as fatigue and the like, observed in the world, would not exist in Brahman.
Why? Because it is heard in scripture that by mere volition—“May I be many, may I procreate”—He brought about the entire creation. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1)

If it is objected: "How can the Śruti speak of that which has been sublated?", he replies with the word "śabda" (scriptural authority). This is because an inconceivable object is known solely through the means of valid cognition that is scripture; and this is observed in the case of the *maṇi* (jewel).

In the beginning of the mantra, the statement "the father-god" (pitṛdeva) refers to the singular location [of the eye]. O Lord, your Veda is the supreme eye for the welfare of the ancestors and the gods.
To the question "Where [is this]? he says: "In the case of an unperceived object," and so forth.
Thus, my statement that the Veda alone is our means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is in accord with the consensus of all;
nothing unprecedented has been asserted by me. //11//

In this regard, since the Vedic word is currently difficult to master and its meaning is hard to comprehend, and since even the sages who determine its meaning contradict one another, it is the very word— consisting of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas— which takes the form of the Veda and determines the meaning of the Veda that must be investigated.

And in that regard, even that word of the Veda which is not personally known by oneself is nevertheless inferable through that [person's] vision; thus, it is established that it alone is the producer of valid cognition.
For it is said thus in the Mahābhārata and the Mānava: "One should augment the Veda by means of Itihāsa and Purāṇa" (Mbh 1.1.267);
and it is called *purāṇa* because of its filling (*pūraṇāt*).
And furthermore, the expansion of the Veda by means of the Āgama is not possible;
for it is not appropriate to fill an incomplete golden bracelet with tin.
Now, if the word "Veda" includes both the Purāṇas and the Itihāsas,
then another Purāṇa must be sought.
If, however, this is not the case, then there would be no non-difference between the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and the Veda. It is replied:

although there is non-difference because the collection of words that conveys a single specific meaning is of non-human (apauruṣeya) origin, the designation of difference is nonetheless justified due to differences in accent and word order.
The non-difference between these two [the Veda and the Upaniṣads] due to their being non-human (apauruṣeya) is revealed in the Mādhyandina recension itself: "Verily, O dear one, the Ṛg-veda,
the Yajur-veda, and the Sāma-veda are the breath of this great Being."
"The Veda, the Atharva-Angirasa, history, and the Purāṇa," and so forth [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10]. //12//
BD: If it is thus, let the investigation of ultimate reality be conducted by means of the *Ṛg-veda* and the other Vedas. To this, he replies: "And in that regard, regarding the word 'Veda'..."
If it is argued that [the Self] exists because of the treatises such as Nyāya which determine the meaning of the Vedas, he replies to that with the words "of those who determine its meaning."
"Of that very [work]" means of that which consists of the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas* and has the nature of the Veda; "he should fully augment" means he should clarify the meaning of the Veda.
From the *purāṇa*, etc. [is the source].
It should be understood that this refers to "the meaning of the Veda.
[The phrase] "with tin" means with lead.
Regarding the status of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas as being of the nature of the Veda:
Someone raises an objection with the words "nanu" (but surely) and so forth;

there, he provides the resolution with the words "ucyate" (it is said) and so forth. [The objection concerns] that collection of words—such as "mṛga" (deer) and so on—which expresses a single referent characterized by all the powers of the Blessed Lord.
Regarding the phrase "the end of the Purāṇas belongs to it":

there is a sequence of accents (*svara-krama*) in the portions consisting of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, but that does not exist in the portion consisting of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; it is by this distinction that they differ.
"Thus indeed," these are the words of Yājñavalkya addressed to his wife Maitreyī:
"O Maitreyī, of this great, all-pervading Lord (īśvara), or of this venerable Being who is established from of old."
The rest is clear in meaning. //12//
Therefore, in the *Skanda-Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-Khaṇḍa*, it is said: "In ancient times, the Grandfather of the immortals performed severe penance;
thereupon the Vedas appeared, together with their six limbs, the Pada and Krama recitations."
Then [he spoke] the entire ancient Purāṇa, which consists of all the scriptures, is eternal,
composed of the word that is perpetual, meritorious, and extends for a hundred crores [of verses].
"Learn of its divisions as they emerged from the mouth of Brahmā:
'The Brāhma Purāṇa is the first,' and so forth.

having heard this, Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, being honored by them yet suspicious of their falsehood, spoke thus to them regarding the Pravargya and the knowledge of Brahman.

"The Śrīmad-Bhāgavata possesses supreme *sāttvika* quality because it is dear to the Blessed One and because it is desired by the devotees (*bhāgavatas*)."
As in the *Padma Purāṇa*, Gautama’s question to Ambarīṣa:

O King, this is the account of the Daitya king and Prahlāda.

"O Ambarīṣa, listen daily to the Bhāgavata as proclaimed by Śuka;

(From the Skanda Purāṇa, Prahlāda-saṃhitā, Dvārakā-māhātmya)

What is the use of hundreds or thousands of other compendia of scriptures,

O Brahmin Nārada, wherever the Bhāgavata scripture may be found in the Kali age, there Hari goes along with the gods.
"O Sage, the person who, being self-restrained, daily recites this verse from the Bhāgavata,

Thus it is established that this must now be investigated.
In Hemādri’s *Vrata-khaṇḍa*:

"Thus, for those deluded regarding the highest good in their actions, the highest good shall indeed be attained in this world;

The work named Bhāgavata is a commentary on the Gāyatrī mantra dedicated to the Blessed Lord (Śrī-Bhagavat).
This is stated in the passage beginning with "yatrādhikṛtya gāyatrīm," and likewise in the Agni Purāṇa regarding it.
This has been explained in detail in the commentary.
Therein, a glimpse of that very commentary is as follows:
"That light is the supreme Brahman, for it is remembered as *bharga*, which means splendor (*tejas*)."
Having begun thus, he spoke again:
"That light is the Blessed Viṣṇu, the cause of the birth and other states of the world."
Some recited Śiva, and some recited the form of Śakti;
some [recited] Sūrya, and some [recited] Agni—the deities of the Agnihotrin priests.

In the concluding statement, "This has been explained" (vibhāsito 'yam), and in the passage beginning with "That pure one" (tac-chuddham), the commentary in the Agni Purāṇa is exactly the same:

however, according to this view, even in the mantra, this word *bharga* is derived precisely from the root *ad* (to eat).

It may be so; however, by the Vedic rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39) and others, one should understand that the substitution of *su* for the second-case singular ending *ām* occurs. "In the Vedas, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas, and likewise the Mahābhārata, Hari is sung of everywhere— in the beginning, in the end, and in the middle.

The Tantra named Bhāgavata,

And that which is indeed praised in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* section of the *Hemādri* compendium, in the context of the gift of Purāṇas, by citing the definition from the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

Regarding this...

The commentary [is composed] by one renowned as an incarnation of Śaṅkara who, out of fear, did not waver from the non-dual doctrine (advayavāda) set in motion by the command of the Lord— whose motives for concealing his own identity will be described—
even though that doctrine describes only a fraction of the vision of the universal form (viśvarūpa) which caused such astonishment in the Queen of Vraja (Vrajeśvarī). Śrī-Vraja...

By describing such matters as the theft of a maiden’s garment in the *Govindāṣṭaka* and other works, he has touched upon them from an objective standpoint merely to ensure the efficacy of his own words. //23//
BD: "For this very reason" means for the reason of excellence [implied by] the characteristics already described;
this Śrī Bhāgavata is to be accepted by both the ancient sages and the most learned of the present day.

Indeed, the Sātvatas relate that it was precisely upon seeing this that the venerable feet of Śrī Madhvācārya, fearing that other Vaiṣṇavas might enter into interpretations following the style of Puṇyāraṇya and others among his disciples, provided instruction on the correct path by writing alternative intended meanings (*tātparya*) for those passages.

Likewise, in the first [verse]:
"The fruit fallen from the wish-fulfilling tree of the Veda,

The Omniscient One, who is exceedingly valiant, having conquered the fourteen-fold conqueror of the directions in fourteen moments,

According to the direction of the verse, "From the second [cause], namely attachment, there arises for one who has strayed from the Lord... the covering of the true nature (*svarūpāvaraṇa*) is that which cannot endure the beginningless aversion of living beings consisting of ignorance regarding the Lord.

He explains that the individual soul (jīva) should worship the Lord with devotion and thereby find love for Him; from that, one becomes liberated from Māyā, having perceived the real difference between the individual soul and the Lord,

"Of the individual soul (jīva)" means "the distinction," that is to say, the difference caused by eternal attributes consisting of the nature of being a servant, being served, atomicity, and omnipresence.

He does not possess eternal knowledge as his inherent nature by which delusion and egoism could be described;
therefore, from that [nature], knowledge arises for him. (Gītā)
From such statements as these,
that which is the reflection of consciousness in *sattva* is precisely [the nature] of that which is conditioned by *sattva*.
If it is argued that his knowledge is such that delusion (*moha*) and egoism (*manana*) would be seen by him in their expanded form, he replies to that with the words "Thus, therefore," and so forth.

Māyā veils the individual soul (jīva) that is already obscured by its aversion to the Lord,

And the Blessed Lord, from time immemorial, is unable to disregard His courtesy toward her, who is devoted and yet possesses authority over the phenomenal world;
likewise, out of fear of her, He [protects] the living beings.
Desiring to bring about their direct encounter, He teaches:
"For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (Gītā 7.14).
From association with the virtuous, discourses that bring knowledge of my prowess become a nectar for the heart and ears;
by relishing them, one quickly enters the path to liberation.
Faith, delight, and devotion will follow in succession;
moreover, it will immediately follow that he taught [this] through his distinctive play in the form of the illustrious Vyāsa.
"Directly for the pacification of what is harmful":
therefore, it should be understood that this [result] is appropriate for both as well.
Now, is it not the case that *māyā* is indeed power (*śakti*), and power is the capacity for causal efficiency?
And since that is a specific attribute (*dharma-viśeṣa*),
how could shame and the like belong to it?
It is said: even though the Blessed One is thus [the ultimate reality], those powers are heard of as having presiding goddesses,
as in the Kenopaniṣad with respect to Mahendra and Māyā.
This is the dialogue. Let that be; we now introduce the subject at hand. //33//

From such statements as "By prostration" (Gītā 4.34),

And from the statement: "By sport" means by way of a sportive incarnation;

[This refers to] a specific attribute (*dharma-viśeṣa*).
The meaning is "like enthusiasm and so forth.

In that regard, although the individual soul (jīva) possesses such a nature of consciousness, it demonstrates that its distinctness from the Supreme Lord is dependent upon Him, as in the phrase "as if deluded. //34//

BD: In that context, by the words "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*) and "and the illusion which rests upon it" (*māyāṃ ca tad-apāśrayām*), [it is shown] that the Lord possesses the power of governing *māyā*, and that the individual soul possesses the state of being governed by *māyā*, as it is deluded by that [illusion].

Thus, these four principles— namely Īśvara, jīva, māyā, and kāla— were perceived by the venerable Vyāsa during his meditative absorption;

Māyā is an insentient substance characterized by the three qualities (guṇas) such as sattva;

Time, however, is a substance that is insentient and is the cause for the conventional usage of "present" and so forth.

Thus, according to the Sūtra, this established state of reality is to be understood as proven by Śruti and Smṛti. //34//

At the very moment when that single Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is enveloped by the locus of *māyā* and consists of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), it simultaneously becomes the object of that *māyā* and is overcome by ignorance (*avidyā*); thus it is said, and the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is understood.
And therefore, by virtue of the difference in the capacity of their own natures, it follows that those two possess mutually distinct natures. //35//
BD: As for [the passages] "One only, without a second" (ChāU 6.2.1), "Consciousness, bliss is Brahman" (BṛhadU 3.9.28), and "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (BṛhadU 4.4.19).
From such scriptural passages as these,
it follows that Brahman— non-dual, pure consciousness devoid of distinctions— is the ultimate reality;
for it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.

Due to the connection with ignorance (*ajñāna*), which consists of the functions of knowledge and nescience and is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), there arose the Lord-consciousness conditioned by knowledge (*vidyopahita*) and the individual consciousness conditioned by nescience (*avidyopahita*). However, Śaṅkara, the possessor of *māyā*, says that there must be an abiding in the nature of non-dual pure consciousness devoid of distinctions;
regarding that, he says: "Whenever indeed... [and so forth].
"Single" is for the sake of clarity.
"Thus it is said" means that [it occurs] simultaneously and quite unexpectedly due to the conjunction with ignorance.
One portion has ignorance as its basis, while the other is overwhelmed by ignorance;
what offense was committed by that Brahmā, such that he became a vessel for the experience of various distractions and afflictions?
Furthermore, since it is impossible to explain the connection with adventitious ignorance, that division cannot be stated according to the aforementioned method;
rather, the meaning is that we have understood it solely through the method perceived by the venerable Vyāsa. //35//
Nor could there be a distinction between those two based on a systematic arrangement such as the reflection of a limited form consisting of varying degrees of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). //36//

BD: However, based on such scriptural passages as "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (RV 6.47.18; BṛhadĀraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), there may be a distinction between the Lord and the individual soul due to the limitation of that non-dual Brahman by means of *māyā*.
In that regard, the Great Lord is the large fragment delimited by *vidyā*, while the individual soul (*jīva*) is the smaller fragment delimited by *avidyā*,
just as [space] is delimited by a jar.
A fragment of space, delimited by a bowl, receives the designation of "large" or "small.
For just as this luminous self, Vivasvat, though one, enters into many forms after piercing through the waters.
"By means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), this unborn Self, the Lord, appears as differentiated within the fields (*kṣetra*).
Since such passages from the *Śruti* speak of that Brahman as a reflection, there would be a division of it [into many]. In the case of knowledge (*vidyā*)...
The Lord is the reflection;
the individual soul (jīva), however, is the reflection in ignorance,
just as [the sun is reflected] in a lake.
Śaṅkara says that just as a reflection in a jar undergoes the designation of "large" or "small," so it is in this case;
he shows the following in order to refute that view with the words "but this is not so."
In this manner, there would be no distinction between the two; such is the logical connection (anvaya). //36//

In that regard, if the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) were real by virtue of being non-illusory (*anāvidyaka*), then it would be impossible for that which is not an object [of cognition] to be the object of delimitation (*pariccheda*).
This is because it is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), and partless (*niravayava*).
And there is also the impossibility of being a reflection,
because of the absence of connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and the absence of any distinction between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
And because it lacks visibility;
for only a reflection is seen, such as that of a portion of light situated in space delimited by a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
But it is not [the case] for space, precisely because of its lack of visibility. //37//
BD: To the question "Why should it not be stated?", he says "In that case, if [there were] a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)," precisely because that is untenable.

He refutes the position that it is a delimitation (*pariccheda*) with the meaning: "given that it is a real entity (*vastu-bhūta*), by virtue of not being non-illusory—that is, by the absence of being constructed by ignorance (*ajñāna-racitatva*), unlike a snake in a rope."
"Of that which is not an object" means "of that Brahman which is untouched by anything," according to the Śruti passage: "It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).

This is what must be understood here: neither the Lord nor the individual soul (jīva) is a specific fragment of Brahman cut off by a real limiting adjunct (upādhi), like a piece of stone split by a chisel;
for Brahman is indivisible.
And because [the Lord] would have to be admitted as being non-eternal,
and because both the Lord and the individual soul would consequently fall into the state of having a beginning;
since for one [of them...]
The cutting is of two kinds, three kinds, or various kinds;
nor is that [individual] merely a specific portion of Brahman conjoined with limiting adjuncts while remaining uncut.

When the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) moves, it is impossible for the portion of Brahman conjoined with that adjunct to move; for since there is a distinction at every moment between the portions of Brahman conjoined with the adjunct, it would follow that [Brahman] would be both conditioned and unconditioned at every instant.
Nor is that [individual soul] the entire Brahman as conditioned,
because the designation of "unconditioned Brahman" would then be untenable;
nor is it the substratum of Brahman.
That [distinction] is merely an adventitious condition (upādhi);
for if it were not, it would follow that the Lord and the individual soul cease to exist in liberation— thus, the doctrine of spatial limitation (paricchedavāda) is trivial.
Now, he refutes the position of the reflection with the words "of that which is devoid of attributes" and so forth.
Because that which is devoid of attributes lacks a connection with the material cause (*upādāna*),
it cannot function as a pervasive image or reflection.

The meaning is that because there is no differentiation and because that which is partless cannot be an object of perception, neither the Lord nor the individual soul (jīva) is a reflection of Brahman.

The meaning is that while the reflection of the sun and other such objects— which are characterized by qualities such as form, which are limited and possess parts— is observed in a medium like water situated at a distance from them, it is impossible to assert such a reflection for Brahman, which is of a nature entirely different from those.

If it is argued that such a reflection of Brahman will indeed occur because a reflection is seen even in space (*ākāśa*) which is of such a nature, [the author] says in response: "due to limiting adjuncts" (*upādhi*); the meaning is "of the orb of light consisting of planets and stars."
Otherwise, that [reasoning] should also be shown to apply to air, time, and space;
for just as there is an echo to sound, so too [is there an image] to Brahman.
He says that there might be a reflection, but that is not tenable;
because it would be a different entity, the theory of reflection is also utterly insignificant. //37//
Likewise, when there is a real distinction and so forth, the abandonment of that [distinction] would not occur merely through the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
If it is argued that the power of the referent of that word (*tat-padārtha*) is the cause in that case, then that is precisely our position.
It is approved by the Teacher. //38//

Because it is impossible to bring about a conjunction between that which is being produced and that which is not being produced,
and because of that,
all those various [appearances] are merely the play of ignorance; thus, by means of this or that [appearance] which has not attained its own true nature...
It is impossible to establish [it]. //39//

BD: Now, under the view that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is non-empirical (*āvidyaka*), he refutes the two theories regarding limitation and so forth with the words "of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ*).
The meaning is: since it is non-empirical, it is false (*mithyātve*), just like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope.
In that regard, because both being delimited by an adjunct (*upādhi*) and being its reflection are untenable, [the reflection] is indeed false; for this reason,
in the case of the space within a jar and so forth, [it is not the space delimited by the jar, nor is it the reflection of the space in the water of the jar...]
Furthermore, by demonstrating through the examples of both the reflection and the space that they consist of real limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),

the doctrine of those who rely on the example of unreal dreams— namely, those who maintain the non-duality of pure consciousness (*cinmātrādvaita*) and are established in the theory of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*)— is not proven.
If the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) were false, then the delimitation and the reflection of Brahman by means of it would both be unreal.
Therefore, the illustration of a real pot and the water within the pot as examples for a false limiting adjunct is indeed inconsistent.
The presentation of the analogy of the jar and the water in the jar is being accomplished;
the presentation of the illustrated subject (dārṣṭāntika) in the form of the activity of the method of knowledge is self-accomplished.
The connection between these two—which would have to be characterized by similarity—is simply impossible to effect, because of the absence of any similarity.
Therefore,
all that— namely, the conceptualization of delimitations and reflected images— is merely the play of ignorance (*avidyā*), the unfolding of nescience (*ajñāna*).
In this manner, that is, by the way thus stated;
by that doctrine of discernment which is unestablished because it has not attained its own nature.
And by that theory of reflection,
it is impossible to establish or demonstrate this or that [distinction].
And therefore, by the logic of "the killer being killed," that classification [of the Vedas] as seen by Vyāsa is certain. //39//

Thus, when the distinction between Brahman and ignorance has been resolved, that very Brahman which, as pure consciousness, is the locus of the absolute non-existence of the connection with ignorance and is therefore pure, becomes the individual soul (jīva) through its connection with that [ignorance] and the resulting impurity.
Furthermore, since that very [consciousness] is the locus of the māyā imagined by the ignorance (avidyā) of the individual soul (jīva), it is the Lord (īśvara);

and since that same [consciousness] is the object of that māyā, it is the individual soul (jīva). Thus, the contradiction would remain exactly as it was. And in that case, ignorance would reside in pure consciousness (cit).

Furthermore, one should consider that such a conception would be inconsistent: namely, that there is "knowledge" (vidyā) in that which is called the Lord (īśvara), even though it is merely an adjunct (upādhi) imagined through ignorance (avidyā); likewise, even while possessing knowledge, it would still be characterized by illusion (māyikatva). Thus, these and other such points are to be reflected upon. //40//
