just as the division of a region of the earth is delimited by water, [so too is the soul].

In this way, it might be a portion of Brahman by means of an adjunct (*upādhi*). No, for there is no apprehension of a portion of Brahman through an adjunct, as there is of a portion of the earth through water; "He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
For such is the Śruti; therefore, there is no such state for Brahman—that is to say, it does not possess limitation by adjuncts (upādhi). This is the meaning.

Alternatively, just as the reflection of the sun in water is perceived as something limited, so too the reflection of Brahman— which is all-pervasive— is not perceived in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
therefore, it is not analogous.
The meaning is that there is no reflection of it.
If so, how are the two treatises to be reconciled?
To this he says, "By the second [verse], regarding increase," and so forth.
That duality does not function in its primary sense; rather,
it functions only by taking up a portion of the qualities (guṇa) characterized by increase and decrease,
just as [the terms] "great" and "small" [apply] to the earth.
Just as two pieces of sugar, or as the sun and its reflection undergo increase and decrease,
so too may the Supreme Lord and the individual soul be.
Why? Because of inclusion;
because the intended meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*) is fulfilled in this respect.
This being so, the meaning is that there is a connection due to the consistency between both the example and the subject (*dṛṣṭānta* and *dārṣṭāntika*). [The word] *pūrva*-...
By means of the primary reasoning (*nyāya*), the two doctrines of determination (*pariccheda*) and so forth are refuted;
however, by means of the subsequent reasoning (*uttara-nyāya*), they are established through figurative application (*gauṇa-vṛtti*).
The opinion of the authors of the Sūtras is that the individual soul (jīva) is either a part of Brahman or its reflection;
likewise, the Lord (īśa) is also either a part of Brahman or its reflection.
This should be understood as the doctrine of the deceitful who are averse to the Lord. //42//

Therefore, the non-dual scriptures [resolve] the contradiction regarding both being of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa) by means of the innate, inconceivable power of the Lord— which is capable of accomplishing the impossible— since the multitude of individual souls (jīva-samūha) is, by their very nature, like the atoms and qualities of His rays, being neither distinct from Him nor non-distinct from Him.

Having set aside these [objections] for now, they must repeatedly be applied later for the purpose of connecting them with the established conclusions obtained through Vyāsa’s meditative concentration. //43//
BD: "Therefore" means precisely because the two treatises beginning with *pariccheda* have been interpreted as having the sense of similarity to that [state];
for instance: "I am indeed You, O Blessed Lord;
You are indeed I; That art Thou."
The [verses] beginning with "ādīni" are non-dual scriptures;
the connection is that these should be applied repeatedly hereafter for the purpose of reconciling this with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Vyāsa’s meditative realization (*samādhi*).
He states the reason for this: "By virtue of both the Lord and the individual soul (jīva) having the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa),
just as in the case of two men— one fair and one dark, or one young and one old."
There is identity through the state of being a Brahmin;
and thus the meaning is that there is non-difference by virtue of the genus (*jāti*) alone, not by virtue of the individual (*vyakti*). Likewise, [the case of] the individual soul (*jīva*)—
Because, by its very nature, through that inconceivable power which is skillful in accomplishing the difficult-to-accomplish for the multitude,
it stands as the locus of the qualities of the atoms of those rays; thus, it exists both as distinct from them and as non-distinct from them.
"Having resolved the contradiction by means of the reason": for the Supreme Lord, indeed, there exists a power called *parā* which is inherent to His own nature, just as heat belongs to the sun.
For it is stated in the wording of the mantra: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and it is innate" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
And because of the traditional teaching: "The power of Viṣṇu is declared to be supreme" (ViP 6.7.61).
For she indeed governs all others besides Him; since... [He is] that.
All other objects exist without ever abandoning their own respective natures;
primordial matter (prakṛti), time (kāla), and action (karma) are unable to touch the Lord, even though He resides within them.
But he remains in his own nature, truly fearing that [state];
and the hosts of living beings, though of the same genus as him, do not associate with him.
However, by depending on Him alone, it obtains its function,
just as the collection of sense organs such as hearing depends on the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa).

Likewise, since that which is dependent on another must have the same nature as that upon which it depends, this lack of contradiction between the scripture of non-duality and the scripture of duality is contingent upon the established conclusion obtained by Śrī Vyāsa through his meditative absorption.
Thus, it is established that there is no difference in the essential nature between the Lord and the individual soul. //43//

Thus, since the distinction between the two is established by virtue of one being the locus of illusion and the other being deluded by illusion, it follows that it is precisely the latter who is the subject to be designated. //44//
The phrase "tad evam" (thus, in that way) is for the sake of clarity;
it means "of that devotee who wards off illusion. //44//
Therefore, because the Blessed Lord alone is the instructor of all that is beneficial, the remover of all suffering,
the supreme essential nature of all things like the sun is to its rays, and the possessor of qualities exceeding all others;
And the purpose, namely "the state of being endowed with supreme love," has been established. //45//

BD: Since the worship of Him is the subject matter because He wards off illusion and delusion, it follows by implication that the Blessed Lord alone is worthy of the love of those who worship Him; thus he says, "Therefore."
Therefore, the connection is that the Blessed One alone is worthy of supreme love, because He is the vessel that wards off illusion and delusion.
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīvātman) is worthy of love, whereas the Supreme Soul, the Blessed Lord, is worthy of supreme love.
In response to the inquiry "Why?", he states the fourfold reason beginning with "all":
"of the rays," and so forth— just as the sun is not the intrinsic nature of its rays, but rather [the source] of the supreme...
The identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) has been refuted by the statement that "the Lord is thus the very essential nature of the individual souls. Furthermore,
from both the Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa and the Saubāla-brāhmaṇa, it is established that the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) possess the relationship of body and embodied.
But he is their embodied self; thus the distinction is clearly known. Therefore, [the power] is superior to all. //45//

In that regard, although he had already perceived the subject matter (abhidheya) as being of such a nature, he nevertheless composed this *Sātvata-saṃhitā* known as the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* for the purpose of engaging others with it; thus he says, "anartha... and so forth.

Devotional yoga (*bhaktiyoga*), characterized by hearing, chanting, and so forth, is *sādhana-bhakti* (the practice of devotion), but it is not characterized by love (*prema*). For while the performance [of practice] depends upon instruction, love depends upon His grace; nevertheless, because that practice has His grace as its cause and contains love as its fruit, it is directly [related to the goal].
Thus it is the pacification of misfortune, and not by way of dependence on anything else;
that which [is achieved] through actions and through austerity.
And as stated in BhP 11.20.32, beginning with "That which [is attained] through knowledge and dispassion," my devotee attains everything directly by means of the yoga of devotion to me.

From such passages as "Heaven and liberation" (BhP 11.20.33), it follows that knowledge and the like are indeed dependent upon devotion; for devotion alone is the path to the highest good, as stated in "Devotion is the path to the supreme goal" (BhP 10.14.4).

Alternatively, the meaning is that the pacification of misfortune—that is, the calamities of saṃsāra—is direct and immediate, whereas the pacification of the dyad beginning with delusion occurs through its own fruit, namely love. Therefore, as before, the subject matter is shown here [in this verse]. //46//
BD: Regarding the word "tatra" (therein): Śrī Vyāsa, although he had already seen [it], beheld it as such, by way of warding off illusion (*māyā*).
Practice is that which is to be accomplished through human effort;
"by His grace" means by the favor of the Blessed One. "Of that" refers to that which is characterized by hearing and so forth.

"By being dependent on other factors" means by way of being an accessory to ritual action (*karma*) and so forth. "But of knowledge and the like," however, refers here to that whose object is Brahman, as stated in the passage: "Brahman is that of which [knowledge] is the [object]. (page 6)

From the word "delusion" (*sammoha*) and so forth, one should understand the conceiving of the self as having the nature of the insentient body and so on. "Hence" (*ataḥ*) refers here to the statement beginning with "disadvantage" (*anartha*). //46//

Now, in order to clarify the purpose of the previous [section] and to manifest that the aforementioned Perfect Person (pūrṇa-puruṣa) is indeed the essential nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the author] indicates His presence therein by way of pointing out the fruit of the work.
Explaining another experience, he says "yasyām" (in which).
Devotion (*bhakti*) is love (*prema*), consisting of the act of hearing (*śravaṇa*). (Page 109)
Because it is to be accomplished through devotion as the means (*sādhana*),
it "arises," meaning it manifests.
He states its incidental quality (*anuṣaṅgika-guṇa*) with the words beginning "śoka" (sorrow).
The implication here is that even their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) perish;
this is because of the words of Śrī Ṛṣabhadeva: "O Vāsudeva, as long as love for me does not arise, one is not released from the bondage of the body" (BhP 5.5.6).
Regarding the Supreme Person— the previously mentioned Perfect Person—
in response to the inquiry as to what His form is, He says: "Kṛṣṇa, indeed, is the Lord Himself," and so forth.

It is that which would be the object of the first cognition for countless people— who have cultivated their inner faculties through thousands of treatises and who, by tradition, are included among those for whom it is well-known— merely upon hearing its name.

Likewise, the meaning is that for one who intends to face [a deity], even a single initial syllable of that name, when employed as a mantra, takes on the form of that [deity]. And they have said regarding the name:
The authors of the Kaumudī state:
"The word *kṛṣṇa* has its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) as the Supreme Brahman, the suckling of Yaśodā who possesses the dark luster of the *tamāla* tree. //47//
BD: Regarding "atha" (now): the purpose is characterized by love for the Blessed One.
"Therein" means: therein, in that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there was another experience on the part of the venerable Vyāsa. This is the meaning.
The meaning is that it "manifests" because it is impossible for love to arise as a separate portion [of the self].
"Of that" refers to love.
The meaning here is that while this love exists, Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Lord Himself; this refers to Śrī Sūta and others, as well as to Śrī Jayadeva and countless other people.
In both instances— "tan-nāma" (that name) and "tan-nāmnaḥ" (of that name)— the name "Kṛṣṇa" is to be understood.
"Rūḍhi" (conventional usage) means [the application of a word] even without the connection between a root and a suffix.
The meaning is that the renown of Yaśodā’s son is like that of the word "maṇḍapa," which refers to a specific type of house. //47//
Then he experienced that very purpose as being even more supreme than the experience of the bliss of Brahman;
for even Śuka, such as he was, [struggled] to attain the excellence of that bliss.
"He taught her that Saṃhitā," he said;
"having first composed it himself in brief and then, following the instruction of Śrī Nārada, having explained it in its proper sequence."

This is the meaning. For this very reason, the fact that the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is heard of here as following the Mahābhārata, and elsewhere that the Mahābhārata follows the eighteen Purāṇas—both of these positions would be reconciled. Because it is immersed in the experience of the bliss of Brahman, it is devoted to renunciation (nivṛtti) and is entirely withdrawn from worldly involvement.
The meaning is: devoted to that, and even unswerving therein. //48//
BD: "Now" (*atha*) means that the venerable Vyāsa experienced its supremacy—that is, its excellence—over the bliss of Brahman, which is the bliss of the reality described as "Brahman.
Such was that...
"Even this experience of bliss"—
the meaning of "for that bliss" (*tad-ānandāya*) is for the sake of attaining the bliss of love for Kṛṣṇa. "For this very reason" (*ata eva*).
"Herein" refers to this *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*; "elsewhere" refers to the *Matsya-purāṇa* and others, where the son of Satyavatī, having composed the eighteen Purāṇas...
"By this [means], he composed the narrative called the Bhārata, augmented by the meanings of the Vedas"—this is the sense.
"Therein" means "in the state of cessation. //48//

Clarifying this very experience born of the meditative absorption of Śrī Vedavyāsa by way of the response to the question of Śrī Śaunaka, he corroborates it with the experience of one who delights in the Self as the all-in-all, together with its underlying reason,
in the verse beginning with "And those who delight in the Self... (Ātmārāmāś ca).

The *nirgranthas* are those who have transcended injunctions and prohibitions, or those from whom the knots of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) have departed. [They follow] that which is causeless, devoid of any connection to results.
Regarding this, he says the following for the purpose of refuting all objections:
Thus, he is one whose nature is to attract even those who delight in the Self (ātmārāma).
He confirms that very point through the experience of Śrī Śuka himself with the words "of Hari's qualities" (*harer guṇa*).
He is one whose mind was previously drawn [to the Lord] by some quality heard from the venerable Vyāsadeva.
Afterwards, he mastered even that which is vast and extensive;
and because of his constant affection for conversation concerning that [Veda], he was one to whom the devotees of Viṣṇu were always dear.
The meaning is that he himself became dear to them.
This is the sense: according to the *Brahmavaivarta*, first of all, starting from the time of his conception...
He understood that Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s voice possesses the power to dispel illusion.
Therein, Śrī Vedavyāsa, desiring to bring him under his influence, recognized that the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam alone is the exclusive means for that purpose, and thus—
Having somehow caused him to hear certain specific verses of his that were filled with the manifestation of extraordinary qualities, and having thereby captivated his mind,
he taught him that very [work] in its entirety; thus [says] Śrī-...
The preeminent greatness of the Bhāgavata has been declared;
thus it is shown that the hearts of the speaker Śrī Śuka and Vedavyāsa are identical.
Therefore, in all cases, the intention (tātparya) must be considered precisely as it corresponds to the speaker's heart, and not otherwise;
whatever else there may be is different from that.
Upon careful reflection, it has been determined that in each case, there is indeed a tendency toward following a wrong path. // 1.7 // Śrī Sūta said: // 49 //

BD: With the words beginning with "him," he states that the object perceived through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is accepted as true by all those who know reality. Regarding the phrase "from which egoism has departed":
this egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is born from the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*); it is not, however, [inherent in the object itself].
It should be understood as being "inseparable from His own nature," since this will be determined in exactly the same way in the second section [of the work].
Regarding the specific verses concerning Him— namely, those on Pūtanā, the Nurse, the Gait, the Bestowing of Boons, and the Charioteership for the Pāṇḍavas— ...
The meaning is that there are several verses demonstrating [Śuka's] role as a doorkeeper and so forth.
In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, Śuka is described as being born from a womb, whereas in the *Mahābhārata*, he is said to be born without a womb (*ayonija*).
The taking of a wife and the continuation of the lineage through daughters—all this is to be reconciled according to the differences in the Kalpas. //49//
Now, in order to determine the purport (*tātparya*) in detail and in due order, as the connection (*sambandha*), subject matter (*abhidheya*),

and purpose (*prayojana*) are to be determined through six compositions, first— regarding that which possesses the relationship of signifier and signified with this scripture, namely, "Dharma, free from deceit," and so forth— [the following is stated].
In the verse, he first states it in terms of its general form: "The object to be known here is the real entity" (BhP 1.1.2).

And here, in this glorious and beautiful Bhāgavata, that which is to be known is the reality that constitutes the supreme truth, and not in the form of substance, quality, and so forth as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; such is this [commentary]. 1.1 Veda-vyāsa 50.

BD: Having briefly stated the relationship (*sambandha*) and so forth, he begins [the detailed exposition] with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so on. "In that very way" (*tathaiva*) means according to the heart-intent of Śrī Śuka and others.
"In general" (*sāmānyataḥ*)...
The meaning is: for the purpose of describing the nature, qualities, and manifestations that have not been previously specified.
"Like the Vaiśeṣikas and others" means like the treatises taught by Kaṇāda and Gautama. //50//
Now, as to what the true nature of that reality is, he says here: "Those who know reality declare that reality is non-dual knowledge" (BhP 1.2.11).
Knowledge is that which has the singular form of consciousness (*cit*).
And its non-duality is due to the absence of any other such or otherwise-natured reality established independently, because it has only its own power as its companion,
and because those powers are not established without that supreme substratum.
By the term "Reality" (*tattva*), its nature as supreme bliss is made known through the indication that it is the ultimate human goal;
for this very reason, of that...
And its permanence has been demonstrated.
1.2. // The son of Śrī. //52//

BD: Having first indicated its essential nature (*svarūpa*), he introduces the statement of the reality (*tattva*) with the words "Now, what... By the phrase "established by itself" (*svayaṃsiddha*), it is indeed meant that which is established by the self alone; for [the term] "self-established" (*svayaṃsiddha*) is used [in this sense]. [The text continues:
"one's own servants... (*svayaṃ dāsāḥ*).
In the expression "tapasvinaḥ" (the ascetics), the state of being a servant through austerity is understood as being accomplished by the ascetic himself;
likewise, such [a state] belongs only to the Supreme Reality, and not even to the individual consciousness (jīva-caitanya). Nor...
That which is not such [as the self] is an insentient entity characterized by primordial matter (prakṛti) and time (kāla).
Because that [insentience] is absent, there is non-duality. How could there be a lack of self-established existence for those two?

To this, he says: "without that supreme support. Even when accompanied solely by its own power, the term "non-dual" (*advaya*) is employed, as in the expressions "the bow is second" or "Pāṇḍu is the second.
But is it not said in the Vedānta that "Brahman is consciousness and bliss"?
Brahman is taught to have the nature of the stream of consciousness; how then is it described here as "knowledge"?
To this, he says: "It is reality."
When it is said, "This is the reality (tattva) here," the word *tattva* is applied to the essential thing;
and for all beings, the essence is indeed happiness.
Because the means have that [liberation] as their purpose;
and thus, its nature as bliss also follows. To the objection that knowledge and bliss are seen to be impermanent, he says: "Precisely for this reason."
The meaning is that it is eternal because it is explained as being self-established;
for indeed, that which exists and is without cause is eternal.
Thus, it has been stated that this treatise belongs to such a Brahmā as described by the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakāra). //51//
Now, it may be objected: cognition is observed to have forms such as blue and yellow and to be strictly momentary;
how, then, is that non-dual, eternal cognition characterized, upon which this treatise is based?
To this he says: "The essence of all Vedānta is that reality which is characterized by the oneness of Brahman; one should be established in that non-dual entity."
Thus, [it is] that whose essential nature is described as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (BhP 12.13.12),
and by the knowledge of which everything becomes known, according to the statement: "By what [being known], the unheard becomes heard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3).
It has been promised by the passage beginning with,
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1),
and so forth; [this refers to] the entirety—
The state of being the sole cause of the world;
as expressed by the passage, "It thought: 'May I become many'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), [this refers to] the True [Self].
And he to whom the state of being a conceptualizer (saṅkalpatā) was imparted,
together with that Brahman who is the greatest of all by virtue of both His essential nature and His powers;

By the designation of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) in the passage "by this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanā*, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), although [the individual soul] is distinct from Him, its designation as the "Self" (*ātmatā*) establishes its extreme non-difference by virtue of being a specific portion of His own nature, according to the reasoning perceived in Bādarāyaṇa’s synthesis.

The oneness of the individual self (jīvātman), when divested [of its limiting adjuncts], is a similarity of form with [the Supreme Self] by virtue of being of the same genus— that is, by having the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa) as a constituent part thereof— as expressed in such passages as "That thou art" (ChāU 6.8.7).
That very characteristic which is the most effective means for first realizing that non-dual reality— the essence of all Vedānta—
is the defining trait of this Śrī Bhāgavata, which is established in and has as its sole object that [reality]; thus it was previously stated.
The connection is with what stands in the verse.
For example, suppose someone, confined within the cave of a house since birth, desiring to know the sun, somehow points out a tiny particle of a sunbeam fallen through a window-lattice.
Someone points it out, saying, "This is that";
the meaning is that, by virtue of its having a form similar to the light of a portion of that [moon], one should contemplate that great orb of light, just as in that case.
Likewise, we shall establish in the Paramātma-sandarbha that the soul's status as a part (aṃśa) of Him is established solely by virtue of its being a particular manifestation of His power.
Thus, the Upanishads teach that it possesses parts (*sāṃśatva*) precisely by virtue of being qualified by aspects characterized as the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth; however,
the scriptural texts teaching its partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) refer to it in its absolute state.

This is the conclusion. Here, the fourth quarter [of the verse], "having liberation as its sole purpose," will be explained in the *Prīti-sandarbha*, because the word *kaivalya* denotes mere purity (*śuddhatva*), and that purity culminates in pure devotion (*śuddha-bhakti*). 12.
13. Śrī-Sūta said: 52.
BD: Establishing that substantial permanence is stable, he states the scripture's specific connection with Brahman, beginning with the words "Now, blue... and so forth.
"By this living self," and so forth;
[this refers to] his statement in the passage concerning the Supreme Deity.

The meaning is that [the Lord is] a specific part of His own self, yet a part distinct from Him, and not a part in the same sense as the fish and other [examples], such as the individual soul (jīvātman). As for the oneness of the individual soul, it refers to the consciousness of the jīva—

The identity of that [individual] with Brahman consists precisely in its having the same form as Brahman by virtue of the universal (jāti) "form-ness" (rūpatva); thus, the distinction between individuals is clearly evident.
This is likewise demonstrated by the example beginning with "just as," and so forth.

This has been shown. "That which is this" refers to the Upaniṣads, such as "He desired, 'May I be many,'" and so forth. That which teaches partlessness is [the teaching of] "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (TaittU 2.1), and "without parts, without activity."

The meaning is that such scriptural passages as "Peaceful, blameless, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19) are devoted exclusively to that [Brahman], being intent solely upon the substantive itself.
That is to say, it declares that Brahman possesses qualities whose specific forms are unmanifested. //52//

In this regard, if the nature of knowledge and eternity of the *jīvātman*— the referent of the term "thou" (*tvam-pada*)— were first to come within the scope of inquiry, then only would the same nature of the referent of the term "that" (*tat-pada*) become easily understood. To bring that about, there is the reflection for another purpose, as stated in [Vedāntasūtra] 1.3.20.
By this reasoning, he states that the individual soul (jīvātman) possesses that very nature:
"The Self was never born, nor will it die; it does not increase."
For those who perform the soma-libations, it is never exhausted despite their transgressions;
rather, the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is everywhere, eternal, and non-falling away—is perceived as mere consciousness, appearing differentiated according to the power of the senses. (BhP 11.3.38)
The self is the pure living being (*jīva*).
It was not born, nor is it born;
precisely because of the absence of birth, its existence immediately thereafter [is likewise absent].
There is not even any modification of characteristics;
it does not increase, it does not grow—
precisely because of the absence of growth.
Even transformation is refuted;
for indeed,
because [these things] are deviant and subject to coming and going, they are like the perceptions of fools—
"Of the bodies of youths and so forth," or "of bodies having the forms of gods, humans, and so forth.
"The knower of the seasons" means the observer of each respective time; the meaning is that the observer of those possessing various states does not himself become subject to those states.
What is this self that is without abode? To this he says: it is mere apprehension, having the singular form of cognition.
Of what nature is it?
[It is] "constantly" (śaśvat), meaning persisting at all times throughout the entire body.
[Objection: But surely [this is not so], because of the cognition that "the cognition of blue has perished" and "the cognition of yellow has arisen."
Regarding the non-departure of knowledge, it is said therein: "by the power of the sense-faculties";
that very knowledge is singular and [arises] through the sense-faculty.
The meaning is that, due to the power [of latent impressions], various conceptual constructions are imagined;
it is only the mental states (*vṛtti*) in the form of blue and so forth that arise and perish, not consciousness itself.
This is the first reasoning (*tarka*), distinguished by the coming and going [of states] and their limits;
the second reasoning should also be understood through the distinction between the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*).
Among those that are variable, [there is] the state—
The example for the possibility of deviation is "just as the vital breath.

Having stated that once the individual self (jīvātman) is known, the supreme self (paramātman) becomes easily known, [the author] introduces the following section with the words "In that regard, if... and so forth, intending to define the individual self for that purpose.
And the Brahma-sūtra states "and [the word] has another meaning. The Dahara-vidyā is recited in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "That which is within this... [Brahma-sūtra 1.3.14].
"Pure is the small white lotus, the dwelling; within it is the small inner space; that which is within that is what must be sought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).
Here, the body of the worshiper is the city of Brahman, and therein—
It is established as the final conclusion that the small Supreme Self (paramātman) residing within the lotus of the heart is said to be the object of meditation;
therein, the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth are taught as that which is to be sought after. Its—

In the middle of that very passage [it says]: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form; it is the Supreme Person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
The sentence has been recited.
Here, the meaning is that the *samprasāda*— the living self (*jīva*) who has attained consciousness— is that very Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) by whom the highest light was reached.

If it is asked for what purpose there is a reference to the individual soul (jīva) within the interval of the discourse concerning the young boy (dahara), he says in response: "for another purpose. In that context, the reference to the individual soul is for the sake of something else.

The meaning is that [the passage] "for the sake of knowing the Supreme Self" refers to that which, having been attained, the individual soul (jīva) becomes fully manifest in its own true nature; that is the Supreme Self.
[The phrase] "it was not born" implies [the stages of] being born, existing, growing, and so forth.

"It undergoes transformation, it diminishes, and it perishes"—thus the six modifications of being (bhāva-vikāra) are enumerated. The collective meaning is that these do not exist for the living self (jīva).
[Objection: But isn't "blue-cognition" and so forth of the nature of cognition?
The self-substance is the knower,
just as the sun, which is the substance of light, is the illuminator; and therefore,
because it is inherent to its own nature, knowledge is eternal for it.

The objectivity (viṣayatā) residing in blue and so forth, which is conveyed by the term "function" (vṛtti) through the channel of the sense organs, perishes precisely upon the disappearance of the blue and so forth. //53//
Explaining the illustration, he shows the perception of the changeless Self through the dissolution of the senses and so forth:
"For the vital breath (prāṇa) indeed pursues the living soul (jīva) here and there, within eggs, embryos, and trees that are not yet fully formed."
When the collection of senses has ceased and the ego is dormant, our recollection of that [state] occurs while remaining as the immutable witness, devoid of any latent impression (āśaya).
[This applies] to those born from eggs within their eggshells.
In the fleshy bodies of those born from a womb;
in trees, which are born from sprouts; and in those that are not clearly determined [as to their origin].
Regarding those born of sweat: it pursues and follows [them].
Having thus demonstrated the state of being changeless in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he now demonstrates it in the case of the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well.
How so?
It is precisely at that time when the collection of sense organs is active in the waking state that the self is perceived as if it were subject to modification.

And when, in a dream, there is the ego (ahaṅkāra) possessed of those latent impressions; but when it is fast asleep— then, while that collection of sense organs has become dormant, subsided, and dissolved, and while the "I" is no longer the ego.
When [the mind] is present or dissolved, the Self remains as the immutable and changeless alone. Why?
Because, apart from the underlying intention (*āśaya*), there is no subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*).
"Without an adjunct" (upādhiṃ vinā) means because of the absence of an adjunct that serves as a cause for modification. [Objection:
But if everything up to the level of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has dissolved, only emptiness (śūnya) remains; where then [is the self]?
The Self is immutable;
therefore, he says: "Our recollection of that.
Of that undivided Self, during deep sleep—
The memory of witnesses—of us who were awake and observing—is born [in the form]: "For such a length of time, I slept happily; I was not aware of anything.
Therefore, [this cannot be the case] for that which was not experienced.
Because that [self] is not remembered, there is indeed such an experience of the Self during deep sleep; however, the sense is that it is not clear due to the absence of connection with objects.
Therefore, regarding the reality that is mere self-luminosity:
It follows that, just like the light of the sun and so forth, the perception of the Self—which consists of perception alone—exists indeed within its own substrate;
and thus says the Śruti: "That which one does not see, [it is] seeing indeed."
"One does not see that which is to be seen, for there is no loss of the vision of the seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).

This is the third inference, distinguished by the division between the witness and the object of witnessing; the fourth inference is likewise to be understood through the distinction between being an object of suffering and being an object of love. //55//

BD: "The illustration" means that because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) maintains a uniform nature across various bodies, it is changeless; [this refers] to that Self (*ātman*). "Of the adjunct" means of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*).
"Due to non-existence" means due to separation. Even then, it should be understood that because of the existence of extremely subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no liberation.
For even when the ordinary ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has dissolved, the referent "I" (*aham-artha*) which is inherent to one's true nature remains; therefore, there is happiness by means of that.
In order to demonstrate that the reflection "I slept" occurs, he says "nanu" and so forth.
The sense is that [the self] is indeed empty [of objective reality], because the self is not perceived apart from the notion of "I.
[This refers to] the undivided self.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: because it is of atomic form (*aṇu-rūpa*), it is incapable of division. Now, one might object: for the self that has arisen from sleep, due to its conjunction with the *ahaṃkāra*, there arises the cognition, "I slept happily."
If it is argued that reflective awareness (vimarśa) is established in the waking state,
whereas in deep sleep it is pure consciousness (cinmātra), the author replies to that with the words:
"Therefore, of that which has not been experienced..."
The meaning is that experience and recollection have a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Therefore, it is established that even in that [recollection], the self is precisely the experiencer.
Now, [if it is argued] that it is merely perception...
It has been stated: "How is its status as the perceiver [established]?
To this he says, "Therefore," and so forth.
As for the phrase "that indeed": that is the Self (ātman).
Consciousness is the agent;
as for the statement that it does not see during deep sleep, that is indeed solely due to the absence of objects to be seen.
But the meaning is not that it is due to the absence of the status of being a seer;
the rest is clear. //54//
Thus it has been said:
"The reasoning known as positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is of fourfold nature;
the first is considered to be distinguished by the presence and absence [of the reason] and its limit."
The second [type of duality] is likewise considered to be the distinction between the seer and the seen;
the third is held by the wise to be the distinction between the witness and the witnessed.
And because it is the locus of love for one who suffers, the fourth [verse] makes happiness known.
Thus, the illustrious Pippalāyana [taught] to Nimi. //55//

BD: In the commentary on the two verses, four logical arguments (*tarka*) have been applied; he points these out with one and a half verses together with the words of experts, beginning with "anvaya" etc.
By the word *tarka*, that which possesses the constituent parts of a logical argument is meant.
Inference is to be understood as follows:
the Self is distinct from the body and so forth, which are seen to be subject to appearance and disappearance and which serve as the locus of suffering; this is known through direct witness.
Because it is the limit of that,
because it is the seer of that, and because it is the witness of that.
"And because it is the locus of love"—thus the reasons are to be understood in sequence; and the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is to be inferred. //55//

The reality that is non-different from the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is the essential nature of such living beings—both by virtue of its very form and because it constitutes their constituent part—is what is to be expressed here; this has been stated by means of a reference to individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*).
For that very reality, designated as the "substratum" (*āśraya*), [is revealed] through the characteristics of the Great Purāṇas.
It is also indicated here by means of a collective enumeration through topics such as creation and so forth; regarding this, he says in two verses:

"Herein are: creation (sarga), emission (visarga), maintenance (sthāna), nourishment (poṣaṇa), the secondary manifestations (ūtayaḥ), the periods of the Manvantaras, the accounts of the Lords (īśānukathā), dissolution (nirodha), liberation (mukti), and the ultimate refuge (āśraya)."

"For the sake of purifying the tenth [discriminative knowledge], the great-souled ones describe here the characteristics of the other nine directly through both scripture and its meaning. (BhP 2.10.1–2). "The Manvantaras and the accounts of the Lords within those Manvantaras" constitute the term *manvantareśānukathāḥ*.
The meaning here is that the ten topics, beginning with creation (*sarga*), are indicated;
and therein, for the sake of purifying the tenth [topic], the reality (*tattva*)—
They describe the characteristic and essential nature of the nine [limbs] for the sake of knowledge.

But surely, it is not understood in this way here; therefore, he says: "By means of what is heard"—that is, by direct verbal statement (*kaṇṭhokti*) itself—in the sections concerning praise and so forth, straightforwardly (*añjasā*).
They describe [the Buddha] directly by means of his actual qualities (*artha*) and through the function of intentional meaning (*tātparya-vṛtti*) in those various accounts. //56//

BD: For the sake of knowing Īśvara, the nature of the individual soul (jīva) has been determined. Now, in order to determine the nature of Īśvara by way of similarity to that [jīva], he applies what was previously stated, beginning with the words "of those who are thus constituted" (evambhūtānām). That which is the nature consisting of pure consciousness (cin-mātra) should be understood as the "conscious subject" (cetayitṛ), because of the previous description.

The meaning is as follows: "ākṛtyā" means by that which is the generic form (*jāti*), namely the state of being a cognizer (*cetayitṛtva*) existing within the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *ākṛti* is used in the feminine sense of form, as well as for generality and body. By "being a part of that" (*tadaṃśitvena*), it means by being a part of the individual soul (*jīva*).
This is the meaning.
That which is non-different from that [Brahman]— that is, the reality of Brahman (brahma-tattva) which is non-different from the individual soul (jīva)—
is indeed a part (aṃśa).

The meaning is that the individual manifestation does not differ from the possessor of the parts. Brahman, possessing powers such as those of the individual soul (jīva), is the collective totality (samaṣṭi); the individual soul, however, is the individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi).
The meaning is that by means of the description of Brahman as such a collective totality, its being of that nature must be stated;
and this applies to the tenth, namely, the Lord (Īśvara).
The remainder is clear in meaning. //56//
In order to clarify that very tenth [topic], he states the seven verses that explain those ten:
"The birth of the elements, the sense-faculties, and the intellect is declared to be *sarga* (creation)."

"The emission [of the world] is known as the work of Puruṣa, resulting from the imbalance of the qualities of Brahman. (BhP 2.10.3) The elements are those beginning with ether (ākāśa), as well as the subtle objects of perception such as sound, and the sense organs.

By the word "intellect" (dhī), the Great Principle (mahat) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) are meant; [they arise] from the transformation due to the inequality of the qualities (guṇas), [proceeding] from Brahman, the Supreme Lord.
Creation (sarga) is the birth of the creator and others;
Puruṣa is Vairāja Brahmā, and that which is performed by him is "pauruṣa" (human/emanated).
The creation of moving and non-moving beings is the meaning of *visarga*;
maintenance is the victory of Vaikuṇṭha, nourishment is His grace,
the *manvantaras* are the true dharma, and the *ūtayaḥ* are the latent impressions of karma.

The accounts of the descents of Hari and the deeds of His followers, as well as stories of the Lord enriched by various narratives, have been proclaimed. The "Victory of Vaikuṇṭha" refers to the exaltation of the created beings through their observance of their respective boundaries.
"Staying" (sthiti) means remaining.
From that [staying] comes his favor toward those who remain as his own devotees, which is their nourishment.
"Manvantaras" refers to the Manus and others who abide in their respective Manvantaras and are favored by him.

The deeds of the virtuous are themselves the Dharma; that which is called "reverence for them" is the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Within that very state of stability, the various karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) are the protective powers (*ūtayaḥ*).

The meaning is that the accounts of the incarnations of Hari while He remains [in the world], and the stories of those who follow Him, are called *īśānukathā*. His *nirodha* (conclusion) is His withdrawal along with His powers (*śakti*) into Himself.

Liberation is the abiding in one's own essential nature after abandoning any other form. Following this state of abiding, there is for the self— the individual soul— a reclining upon Hari together with his own powers, which serve as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The meaning is that "lying down" (śayana) refers to cessation (nirodha) by virtue of following Hari’s own lying down;
therein, Hari’s lying down is the closing of the eyes toward the phenomenal world (prapañca).

The "sleeping" of living beings therein should be understood as their dissolution. Liberation is the state of being established in one's own true nature, having abandoned ignorance, lack of knowledge, and so forth—which are superimposed by avidyā and take on other forms—within that very cessation. //57//

BD: He explains the ten [topics] beginning with creation by means of the passage starting with "tad evam" (thus, in this way). "From Brahmā, the Supreme Lord" refers to the supreme lordly creation of the cause.

The meaning is that the creation of effects belongs to Vairiñca (Brahmā). Regarding "liberation": having abandoned the state of gods, humans, and so forth—which is a form fabricated otherwise by ignorance following from aversion to the Blessed One—[one attains it] through devotion to Him, which proceeds toward His favor.

Having destroyed [the body], the establishment of the individual soul (jīva) in its own nature—characterized by the eight qualities such as freedom from sin—is the "qualified" state; this means that liberation is the state of remaining in the presence of the Lord, devoid of any return [to saṃsāra]. //57//
Since manifestation and cessation exist and are determined from it,
that substratum is designated as the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Manifestation (*ābhāsa*) means creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
From which cessation and dissolution arise,
it is determined, perceived, and shines forth within the cognitive faculties of living beings.
That which is well-known as Brahman and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is called the substratum;
the word "iti" has the sense of "in this manner."
Therefore, [the term] "Bhagavān" [is used]; its detailed exposition shall be provided later. //58//
BD: Now, with nine verses beginning from the [fifty-eighth], he states the reality of the substratum (*āśraya-tattva*) which is to be characterized: "And appearance...
The word *yataḥ* is used in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) to express cause (*hetau*). //58//

And regarding that state, in order to clearly demonstrate the nature of the substratum even by way of the individual (vyaṣṭi) through direct experience, he states the division into the internal (adhyātma) and so forth:
"This person who is internal is indeed that same one who is divine (adhidaivika)."
That which is the cessation of both there is indeed the person belonging to the elemental realm (ādhibhautika).
"When we do not perceive any one of the three when the others are absent,
he who knows that triad is the Self, the support of its own substratum.
This person who is internal, the seer and individual soul (jīva) who identifies with the instruments such as the eyes— [is that Self].
Thus, the divine [agent] is the sun and so forth, who presides over the eyes and other senses;
for prior to the creation of the body,
the instruments (karaṇas) are incapable due to the absence of a presiding authority, and thus there is no manifestation of the instruments.

Because there is no arising of distinct functions for either of those two— the one conceiving itself as the agent and its assistant— there is no difference between them other than their common state as individual souls (*jīva*).
Consequently, both consist of the form of the deity who presides over the instrument and the one who conceives itself as that instrument.
Since separation is of two kinds,
that which is physical (ādhibhautika)— characterized by the eyeballs and so forth, the visible body— is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the person (puruṣa), that is, the individual soul (jīva).
For there is the scriptural text beginning with, "This very person consists of the essence of food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). //59//
BD: [Objection: But how can the individual soul (jīva), who identifies with the instruments, be the impeller of the sun and other luminaries which are those very instruments?
To this he replies: "prior to the creation of the body" and "of the instruments. This is because, prior to that, there is no locus [for their operation].
The meaning is: "due to the absence of the eyeball and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because the differentiation of the activity (vṛtti) does not arise for either of those two":
the activity of the instruments (karaṇas) is the grasping of their respective objects.
The function of the deities there, however, is that of instigators.
This is the essential point here: even prior to the arising of the body, the sense-faculties and their respective deities already exist together with the living soul (jīva).
At that time, because they lack a means of subsistence (vṛtti), their inclusion within the individual soul (jīva) is intended;
however, when the body has arisen, there occurs a distinction between those two, as he says: "And therefore, both... (verse 59).

The phrase "the absence of one [implies] the other" demonstrates that since these are established in mutual dependence, they lack a common substratum. For instance, without the object of perception, the instrument—which is to be inferred from the cognition thereof—is not established;
nor is there a perceiver, and without that [perceiver], the presiding agent who is to be inferred from the operation of the instrument is not established.

The sun and so forth; for without that [sun], the instrument does not function, and without that [instrument], the object of sight is not perceived. Thus, in the absence of either one, we do not perceive the other.
In that state, at that time, he who knows— that is, perceives— as a witness that triad by means of a cognition consisting of mere observation, is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

It is the substratum (*āśraya*). Since these [other factors] also possess mutual substratum-ship, in order to exclude that, the qualification "having its own substratum" (*svāśraya*) is used, meaning "not having another as its substratum" (*ananyāśraya*).
And it is both that [substratum] and the substratum of others.
In that regard, the locus [of the relationship] is stated by accepting the aspect of non-difference between the part (the individual soul) and the whole (the Supreme Self), as in the verse:
"Therefore, even the other considers it a misfortune" (BhP 1.7.5).
Furthermore: "The waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states are the functions of the intellect according to the qualities [of nature]."
"The individual soul (jīva) is distinct from them and is intended as the witness" (BhP 11.13.27); thus,
one should not suspect that the pure jīva— referred to by the term "witness" in such passages as "the pure one beholds the impure agent" (BhP 5.11.12)— is the substratum [of these qualities].
Alternatively, is it not the case that internal factors and so forth also possess the status of being a basis?
True; nevertheless—

Because they are mutually dependent, there is no absolute state of being a substratum (*āśrayatākaivalya*) therein; thus he says "one" (*ekam*), meaning that those [faculties] are not primarily designated by the word "substratum.
Well then, let the witness (*sākṣin*) alone be the substratum.
Regarding this, he says "the triad":

that [Self] is the Witness; but the individual soul (jīva) is that which has its own self as its support and no other support—that is, one whose support is precisely the Supreme Self (paramātman) itself. Thus it is.
And it will be said in the *Haṃsaguhyastava*:
"The person knows everything, yet the knower of that does not know the qualities; I praise the omniscient and infinite One" (BhP 6.4.25).
Therefore, as stated in the passage beginning with "and the reflection," the Supreme Self alone is the substratum. //2.10// Śrī-
Śuka //60//

BD: He explains with the words "one by one" (*ekam ekatarety*) and so forth that because the three—beginning with the internal (*ādhyātmika*)—are established through mutual dependence, they lack the status of being a foundational basis (*āśrayatva*).
The triad consists of the internal and the others.

The triad. [Objection: Since the pure soul (jīva) is established as being independent by the designation of its status as the witness (sākṣin) of the body, senses, and so forth, why do you not state that it is the substratum (āśraya)? To this he says: "In this case, of the part and the whole.
The meaning is that here the part is also included within the whole.
"Or else" (*athavā*) indicates another interpretation due to dissatisfaction [with the previous one]. "Then" (*tarhi*) refers to the witness, the pure *jīva*.
"All" (*sarvam*) refers to the person, the *jīva*. //60//

While describing the characteristics that manifest the status of this Śrī Bhāgavata as a Mahāpurāṇa in another manner, he states its very basis in two verses: "Creation, then dissolution, the activities, protection, and the intermediate periods..."
The lineage, the history of the lineage, the constitution, the cause, and the refuge.
Those who know it declare that the Purāṇa is endowed with ten characteristics;
O Brahmin, some say it is fivefold, according to the distinction between the great and the small.
The intermediate periods are the Manvantaras.
It is fivefold:

primary creation (sarga), secondary creation (pratisarga), genealogy (vaṃśa), the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties (vaṃśānucarita); such is the Purāṇa characterized by these five marks.
Thus some say;
and that difference of opinion is based on a distinction of scope— determining whether something is a *mahāpurāṇa* or an *alpapurāṇa* according to the criteria of being "great" or "small."
Although all ten of those [qualities] are also observed in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other texts,
they are nevertheless few in number because only five are mentioned as primary; whereas here, all ten are present.
The inclusion of all objects within the aggregates in their respective order was not intended [here],
because those objects number twelve.

Those [factors] mentioned in the second chapter do not correspond in number with those in the third chapter and subsequent ones; likewise, cessation and the others do not correspond with those in the tenth chapter and so forth, with the exception of the eighth.
This also applies to the others.
Because it is simply impossible for others to enter [it] due to their possessing the characteristics as previously described;
this was stated by the venerable Śrī-Svāmī himself:
"In the tenth [canto], the suppression of wicked kings, which is the cause of the decline of dharma, is described for the purpose of spreading the excellent fame of Kṛṣṇa; thus,
the fourfold suppression beginning with that of the *prākṛta* has been described."
Therefore, in this section (skandha), it is intended by them that the primary focus of the description is the very locus of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form.
And he himself has stated: "In the tenth [skandha], the tenth objective is the relationship between the locus and that which rests upon it."
Regarding the term "vigraha":
in this manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well.
Therefore, for the most part, all meanings [are to be understood] in all [instances].

It is their intended position that [the aggregates] are thus defined as either qualities or as primary entities within the aggregates; and in the phrase "directly by means of the heard and the meaning," it is understood in exactly that way, since such [definitions] are possible in every instance.
Consequently, even the first and second [Purāṇas] would have to be included among the Mahāpurāṇas;
therefore, the sequence has not been adopted. //61//
BD: "Asyeti" means "in another manner," which implies that in some cases there is a difference in name and a difference in meaning.
Some of dull intellect apply these ten characteristics sequentially to the third [chapter] and so forth;
refuting them, he says: "Of those mentioned in the second chapter. Eighteen...
It should be understood that [otherwise] the characteristics of the *Bhāgavata*—namely, its consisting of one thousand verses and its division into twelve *skandhas*—would be contradicted;

furthermore, the statement that it is the *Bhāgavata* at the conclusion of the chapters would not be possible. If the *Bhāgavata* were merely that which was spoken by Śuka, then [the same would apply to] the first [book] and the remainder of the twelfth.
There is no contradiction with reality.

Therefore, the eighteen-thousand [verse] work was studied and recited by Śuka from his father, the Teacher; thus, at present, these traditions are likewise established as beginningless. This is the conclusion. //61//
Now he describes the characteristics of creation and so forth:
"The emergence of the unmanifest, the agitation of the guṇas, the tripartite mahat, the ahaṃkāra, and the elements, subtle elements, senses, and objects is called creation. (BhP 12.7.11)
From the agitation of the qualities of Pradhāna arises Mahat; from that arises the threefold Ahaṃkāra; from that, the elements—
The "origination" (sarga) is the manifestation of the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma), the sense organs (indriya),
the gross elements (sthūla-bhūta),
and the deities presiding over them.
The meaning is that "creation" (sarga) refers to the creation of causes;
this consists of latent impressions (vāsanā) belonging to those who are favored by the Puruṣa.
This emission is a collection; from seed to seed is all that is moving and unmoving.
The Puruṣa is the Supreme Self (Paramātman) of these [elements], beginning with the Mahat.
This aggregate, dominated by the latent impressions of the soul's prior karma,
is the effect in the form of moving and non-moving living beings, proceeding from seed to seed.
The emission that has entered into a continuous flow is called *visarga*;
the meaning is the emission of individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*). By this, the root *ut* [is explained].
It was said:
"The conduct of living beings—both mobile and immobile—has been ordained by Himself for men, whether through their own desire or by means of scriptural injunction. (BhP 12.7.13)
For moving beings, the sustenance generally consists of non-moving things,

and by the use of "and" (ca), moving things as well; however, in the case of humans, that fixed mode of subsistence arises either from their own nature, from desire, or even from scriptural injunction.
The meaning is that it is called "livelihood" because it is made for the sake of one's subsistence;
it is the desire to protect, preserve, and bring down those who have fallen, throughout every age after age for the sake of the entire world.
"By whom the enemies of the three Vedas are slain among animals, mortals, sages, and gods"— by these incarnations; by this,
the story of the Lord [is told].
The triad of abode, nourishment, and so forth has been described.
The Manvantara, the Manu, the gods, the sons of the Manu, the lords of the gods, the sages, and the partial incarnations of Hari are said to be the sixfold [manifestation]. (BhP 12.7.15)

The meaning is that by the mention of the conduct of Manu and others, the True Dharma (saddharma) alone is intended here; consequently, there is consistency with the preceding text. The lineage of kings born of Brahman is the ancestral succession throughout the three periods of time.

"The lineage history of those kings, their conduct, and those who were the sustainers of their lineages"—this refers to the conduct (*vṛtta*) and the lineage history (*vaṃśyānucarita*) of those kings and those who were the sustainers of their lineages. 62.

BD: In order to show the definitions of the creation and so forth that were enumerated, he says "atha" and so on. It should be understood that the term "avyākṛta" (unmanifested) is an adjective qualifying even "mahat" (the Great Principle). As it is said: "The Great Principle is threefold: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa" (ViP 1.2.34).
Thus, from the *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava*:
it should be understood that the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, resides within Viriñca.
The remaining [verses] have clear meanings. //62//

"Dissolution is of four kinds by its very nature: occasional (*naimittika*), elemental (*prākṛtika*), constant (*nitya*), and absolute (*ātyantika*); thus it has been declared by the wise to be 'rest' (*saṃsthā*) for this [Lord].
(BhP 12.7.17) "Of this" refers to the Supreme Lord.
"By nature" means by power;
by the term "ultimate," liberation is also included herein.

The cause of this creation and so forth is the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the agent of ignorance and karma; others call it the "possessor of latent tendencies" (*anuśayin*) or the "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*).
Here, "cause" (*hetu*) means the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Of this universe;
for by means of ignorance, he is the agent of action,
whom some call the "one with residual impressions" (anuśayin) due to the predominance of consciousness.
Others say it is "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) by virtue of the predominance of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
That [Self] whose presence and absence [are observed] throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—
"That Brahman is the refuge within the functions of the individual soul (*jīva*) which are composed of *māyā*. (BhP 12.7.19).

Here, because it would contradict the meaning obtained through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Śrī Bādarāyaṇa, the pure essential nature (*śuddha-svarūpa*) of the individual soul is not explained as the refuge; rather, this is precisely the intended meaning.

That Brahman is the [reality] of living beings, which possesses a distinction from them by its own pure nature throughout the states such as waking, and also throughout the substances beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), which are composed of illusion and fashioned by the power of Māyā; yet it also possesses a continuity with them by way of being their supreme witness.
In the various modes of existence— whether functioning as the pure essential nature or functioning with adjuncts— the term *apāśraya* means that which is the support by transcending everything;
for the word *apa* signifies exclusion (*varjana*), and exclusion is...
And since it culminates in transcendence,

he thus describes— by means of two verses— the knowledge of the pure essential nature of the individual soul (jīva), which is designated by the word "cause" and serves as the door for the manifestation of its refuge.
Just as substance is the sole essence among categories, so too is the "mere-that" (tanmātra) the sole essence within names and forms;
for within those five states beginning with the seed, there is both conjunction and disjunction.
When the mind, having abandoned the three modes of activity by itself,
or through yoga, ceases to identify with them, it then turns away from this body.
Just as in objects consisting of form and name, such as jars and the like, there is the substance of earth and so forth, which is inherent within them.
And it is ten thousandfold,
because it is perceived even without the view of an object;
thus, it is merely that.

The pure reality, which is merely the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-caitanya*), is joined with ignorance (*avidyā*) throughout all nine states beginning from conception and ending with death, though it is inherently unjoined; having thus known the pure Self, one becomes despondent with worldly existence and fit for seeking refuge— this is what is meant by "one should desist."

The three states of existence consist of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. One should realize the Self, which is the Supreme Self, by oneself through the contemplation of its being composed of Māyā— like Vāsudeva and others— or by means that are not fixed, like Deva Tyādi and others.
Or by means of yoga; and therefore, here [the cessation] of exertion other than the cultivation of that [yoga]. 1.7. Śrī Sūta said: The connection has been stated. 63.

BD: In the previously mentioned [system of] ten characteristics (*daśalakṣaṇī*), liberation (*mukti*) was a single characteristic; however, in this [system of] fourfold states, liberation—designated as absolute dissolution (*ātyantikalayā*)—has been brought forth. And regarding the term "one who possesses latent dispositions" (*anuśayin*): the individual soul (*jīva*) characterized by the remnants of karma that have been experienced is called "one who possesses latent dispositions. Regarding the word "form" (*rūpa*)...
The meaning is: "in those [entities] endowed with both form (mūrti) and designation (saṃjñā).
The meaning of "the perception of an effect" is that even when separated from jars and the like, earth and so forth are still perceived.
"By taking refuge" means that one becomes fit for the meditation on the Lord (Īśvara).
"By oneself" refers to Vāmadeva, who indeed realized the Supreme Self even while still in the womb; by means of yoga, he became a god—this is the meaning. //63//

Thus concludes the *Śrī Bhāgavata-sandarbha*, which contains the essence of the teachings of Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana— who were honored by the assembly of all the kings of Vaiṣṇavas and who were followers of the feet of the divine Lord Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, the incarnation whose purpose was to purify the Kali-yuga through his own worship and distribution [of the scriptures].
The first compendium, named Tattva-sandarbha.

BD: Thus, [the term] *kali* refers to that which purifies the Kali-yuga; His incarnation—that is, His manifestation—has as its purpose the *vibhajana*, or the detailed exposition, of one's own worship (*sva-bhajana*).
Of Him, the Śrī-Bhagavat...

Śrī Rūpa and [Sanātana], who were the attendants at the feet of Lord Kṛṣṇacaitanya and who served as the vessels for the hospitality and honor accorded in the assemblies of all the kings of Vaiṣṇavas throughout the world.
In that [work] whose womb— the interior— consists of the instructional verses of the two eternal Anuśāsana and Bhārata.
This commentary on the *Tattva-sandarbha*, composed by Vidyābhūṣaṇa and interspersed with the readings of Śrījīva, should be refined by the virtuous.
Thus ends the *Tattvasandarbha-ṭippaṇī* composed by the illustrious Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
